nature-eco-323.title: Are humans apex predators?
nature-eco-323.text: Are humans apex predators? A 2013 study averaged the trophic levels of foods in the human diet and found a mean of 2.21. Values ran from 2.04 in Burundi to 2.57 in Iceland. That puts people level with non-apex animals such as the anchovy or the pig. A 2014 critique looked at the sea instead. Humans eating mainly predatory fish in two marine systems had trophic levels of 4.65 and 4.5, making them apex predators there. The answer depends on whether land-based diets or marine food webs are measured, and ecologists still disagree.

nature-eco-322.title: Mesopredator release: when the middle hunters take over
nature-eco-322.text: Removing badgers in a trial against bovine tuberculosis, a cattle disease, more than doubled hedgehog densities. That is mesopredator release: the rise in mid-sized predators once the top predators that kept them in check are removed. Over the past two centuries in North America, the ranges of all apex carnivores have shrunk, while those of 60% of mesopredators have grown. The same happens at sea. Hunting of sperm whales, with a trophic level of 4.7, has increased populations of large squid.

nature-eco-408.title: Are trophic cascades weaker on land?
nature-eco-408.text: The earliest documented trophic cascades were all in water, which led to speculation that cascades are mainly an aquatic phenomenon. The debate over terrestrial trophic cascades asks whether cascades on land are as strong as those in lakes, streams and seas. A 2002 meta-analysis found them generally weaker on land, with smaller changes in plant biomass. A 2009 study, however, found many tree species heavily affected by the loss of an apex predator. Critics note that real food webs blur trophic levels through omnivory, diets that change as animals grow, and food arriving from outside. Studies still disagree.

nature-eco-355.title: Foundation species: the builders of communities
nature-eco-355.text: Corals, kelps, oysters, seagrasses, mangroves and forest trees build the places where other organisms live. They create habitat and ease physical stresses such as waves and drying. Each is a foundation species: a species that plays a strong role in shaping the structure of its community. Paul K. Dayton coined the term in 1972 for certain marine invertebrates and algae. Foundation species can sit at any trophic level, as producers, herbivores or predators. They do not always add variety. Studies removing creosote bush and eastern hemlock found that the number of species rose afterwards, suggesting foundation species can sometimes limit diversity.

nature-eco-358.title: The green world hypothesis: why herbivores haven't eaten everything
nature-eco-358.text: Why has the world stayed green? In 1960 Hairston, Smith and Slobodkin offered an answer: predators keep down the herbivores that would otherwise eat the vegetation. Their idea is the green world hypothesis, also called the HSS hypothesis after its authors. Sea otter studies support it. Otters eat sea urchins, and without otters, urchins nearly eliminate the kelp, leaving urchin barrens. A rival idea, the plant self-defense hypothesis, says plants survive mainly through thorns, toxins and tough tissues. The two explanations still compete.

nature-eco-364.title: The inverted biomass pyramid of the sea
nature-eco-364.text: In the sea, consumers can outweigh the producers that feed them. Their total mass can exceed that of the producers, turning the usual biomass pyramid upside down. The reason is speed. Ocean producers are tiny, fast-reproducing phytoplankton, so a small mass can sustain a high rate of primary production. Land producers such as mature forests need far more mass for the same output. As a result, zooplankton make up most marine animal biomass, and they link phytoplankton to the rest of the food web.

nature-eco-365.title: The whale pump: fertilizing the ocean surface
nature-eco-365.text: In the Gulf of Maine, whales carry more nitrogen through their feces than all the rivers in that system combined. Whales feed deep down, where krill, small shrimp-like animals, are found, but return regularly to the surface to breathe. The whale pump is this upward delivery of nutrients from the depths. It reverses the usual downward flow of the ocean's {{ref:nature-eco-204}}, in which sinking particles drift from surface to bottom. Whale feces are up to 10 million times richer in iron than seawater. In the iron-poor Southern Ocean, that iron feeds phytoplankton.

nature-eco-330.title: Cascade effects: one loss triggers many
nature-eco-330.text: When sea otters were hunted for their pelts, urchins stripped the kelp. The barrens left behind lost urchins and kelp-dependent species alike. That is a cascade effect: a chain of secondary extinctions set off when a key species in an ecosystem dies out. The main cause is the loss of top predators. Their prey multiply, overuse their food and then crash. The species most at risk depend on a few foods, rely on the lost species, or must live alongside an invading species.

nature-eco-345.title: Why energy moves more efficiently in the sea
nature-eco-345.text: Energy passes between trophic levels more efficiently in the sea than on land. Transfer from phytoplankton to herbivorous zooplankton is estimated at about 20%, compared with 10% on land. Phytoplankton biomass can turn over 100–300 times a year, while land plants turn over only 0.5 to 2.0 times. The number of levels shapes what the sea can support. Coastal upwelling zones, where deep water rises, may have as few as three trophic levels and support whales. Open oceans can have six and support only small tuna and squid at the top.

nature-eco-344.title: The ten percent law of energy transfer
nature-eco-344.text: Start with 10,000 J, or joules, of sunlight. Plants take 100 J, a deer that eats them gets 10 J, a wolf 1 J, and a human eating the wolf just 0.1 J. That standard example shows the ten percent law. This rule of thumb says that only about ten percent of food energy passing up one trophic level is stored as new flesh. The rest is lost in transfer, used in respiration or lost through incomplete digestion. The rule is credited to Raymond Lindeman (1942). Yet he did not call it a law, and he cited efficiencies from 0.1% to 37.5%.

nature-eco-347.title: Ecological stoichiometry: the chemistry of eating
nature-eco-347.text: Termites have a carbon-to-nitrogen ratio of about 5, yet they eat wood with a ratio of 300–1000. Ecological stoichiometry studies mismatches like this: how the balance of energy and chemical elements shapes living things and their interactions in ecosystems. Plants and algae vary widely in their elemental make-up. Animals keep a nearly fixed composition, a trait called stoichiometric homeostasis. In lakes, algae and detritus, dead organic matter, range in carbon-to-phosphorus ratio from 100 to 1000. The zooplankton Daphnia stays near 80:1. Nitrogen and phosphorus pollution from farming can boost stream producers and ripple up the food web.

nature-eco-373.title: The Redfield ratio: the ocean's chemical recipe
nature-eco-373.text: Phytoplankton and the deep ocean's dissolved nutrients share one recipe: carbon, nitrogen and phosphorus in the ratio 106:16:1. This is the Redfield ratio. Alfred C. Redfield proposed that phytoplankton needs control the ocean's ratio, since they release nitrogen and phosphorus when they are broken back down into dissolved form. It became a fundamental principle of marine ecology and of biogeochemistry, the study of how chemicals move between living things and their surroundings. It is not universal. {{ref:nature-eco-394}}, {{ref:nature-eco-396}} and changing nutrient inputs can shift it.

nature-eco-341.title: Decomposition: how the dead feed the living
nature-eco-341.text: Earth's living matter is finite, so it must be used again and again. Decomposition makes that possible. It is the breakdown of dead organic matter into simpler substances such as carbon dioxide, water, simple sugars and mineral salts. It is part of the {{ref:nature-es-084}}. Some decomposition is abiotic, driven by chemical or physical processes. Biotic decomposition, or biodegradation, is carried out by living things, mainly microbes. Plant matter breaks down in stages. First, water leaches out soluble compounds, and the material breaks into fragments. That gives the organisms feeding on it more surface to attack. Vertebrate bodies pass through five stages: fresh, bloat, active decay, advanced decay and dry remains. Where decomposition slows, carbon piles up. Waterlogged soils slow it, so carbon-rich sediments build up and act as a long-term {{ref:nature-eco-169}}. People depend on this process too. Ecosystems that lose biodiversity provide fewer services, including decomposing waste.

nature-eco-402.title: Soil organic matter: the living and dead fraction of soil
nature-eco-402.text: About 70% of the world's organic carbon in soil lies below 20 cm depth. That carbon belongs to soil organic matter, the organic part of soil: plant and animal remains at various stages of decay, soil microbes, and the substances they make. It improves soil structure, water retention, pollutant retention, pH buffering, nutrient cycling and the variety of soil life. It raises fertility in two ways. It holds nutrients on exchange sites, and it slowly releases nitrogen, phosphorus and sulfur as it mineralizes. Microbes break plant litter into minerals that plants can absorb, a step called mineralization. Part of the litter becomes {{ref:nature-eco-403}}, a stable form, instead. Organic matter is usually estimated to be 58% carbon, so measuring a soil's organic carbon often stands in for measuring the matter itself. Climate decides where it builds up. It accumulates where cold or wet conditions slow the organisms of decay, and it breaks down fast in hot, rainy tropical climates.

nature-eco-393.title: Soil biology: the hidden life underfoot
nature-eco-393.text: A teaspoon of productive soil holds 100 million to 3 billion bacteria. A gram of garden soil can hold around 700 km of fungal hyphae, the thin threads that fungi grow. Soil biology is the study of this life, from bacteria and fungi to earthworms and burrowing mammals, and of what it does. Soil organisms break down organic matter and release nutrients for plants. That work shapes fertility, soil structure and carbon storage. Nutrients held in their bodies are protected from leaching, being washed away, especially nitrogen and phosphorus. Earthworms, ants and termites reshape their habitat. They mix soil, help water soak in and enrich it with nutrients. Saprotrophic fungi, which feed on dead matter, turn it into stable organic matter and mineral nutrients such as nitrate and phosphate. Much about how soil populations function and interact is still unknown.

nature-eco-340.title: Decomposers: the recyclers of the living world
nature-eco-340.text: Plants cannot move to find nutrients or digest other organisms, so they rely on decomposers to free nutrients from dead matter. A decomposer is an organism that breaks down dead organisms and releases their nutrients into the surroundings. The word names a role in an ecosystem, not a particular kind of organism. Fungi and bacteria digest food outside their bodies. Invertebrates such as earthworms digest it inside and release nutrients in their feces. In forests, fungi are the main decomposers. Only wood-decay fungi have the enzymes to break down lignin, the tough material in wood, and their hyphae can penetrate large pieces of wood. By breaking down the dead, decomposers return carbon to the air and recycle nutrients into forms plants can use.

nature-eco-404.title: The soil carbon pool: Earth's biggest living-world carbon store
nature-eco-404.text: The world's soils hold an estimated 2,500 gigatons of carbon. That is 3.3 times the 750 gigatons in the atmosphere and 4.5 times the 560 gigatons in living things. This soil carbon pool is a key part of the global {{ref:nature-eco-164}}. About 1,550 gigatons of it is organic carbon, mostly in soil organic matter. Carbonates, mineral forms of carbon, make up the rest. The pool can move either way. Depending on outside factors, soil can soak up and store carbon, or release it as heat-trapping gases.

nature-eco-298.title: Detrital food webs: the economy of the dead
nature-eco-298.text: Leaf litter, dead wood, carrion and dung are all detritus: non-living organic matter. A detrital food web starts there. Decomposers break detritus down and pass it on to detritivores, which carnivores then eat. This web is joined to the grazing web of living plants. Mushrooms from decomposers feed deer, squirrels and mice, and robins eat earthworms that feed on leaves.

nature-eco-401.title: Dark earths: fertile soils made by people
nature-eco-401.text: Amazonian Dark Earth was made on purpose. Indigenous communities created it, and it contrasts sharply with the poor, weathered soils around it. Dark earths are dark, carbon-rich, highly fertile soils, many of them created or enriched by human soil management. The practice is not confined to the Amazon. In Ghana and Liberia, combining different wastes produces African Dark Earths rich in calcium, phosphorus and carbon. How large Amazonian societies were before 1492, and how far Dark Earth shaped them, are continually debated.

nature-eco-342.title: Rate of decomposition: why some things rot faster
nature-eco-342.text: Dead animals decay faster than leaves, and leaves faster than branches. The rate of decomposition, how fast dead material breaks down, is governed by the physical environment, the quality and amount of the material, and the microbes present. Decomposition is fastest in damp conditions with enough oxygen, and slow in very wet or very dry soils. Labile, or easily broken, compounds such as sugars go fast. Recalcitrant, or resistant, ones such as lignin persist. Litter rich in lignin therefore decays slowly, and low-lignin plant communities cycle nutrients faster. Tilling speeds decomposition by adding oxygen and exposing new organic matter to microbes.

nature-eco-403.title: Humus: the stable dark heart of soil
nature-eco-403.text: A small share of soil does an outsized job. Humus is usually five percent of soil or less by volume, yet it is an essential nutrient source and improves soil texture. It is organic matter that soil organisms have broken down to the point where it resists further decay. Its capacity to hold charged nutrients, both cations and anions, is many times greater than that of clay on a dry-weight basis. Humic substances are classed as fulvic acid, humic acid and humin, in order of rising molecular weight and resistance to microbes.

nature-eco-405.title: Mineral-associated organic matter: carbon locked in soil
nature-eco-405.text: Some carbon in soil lasts for centuries, while some is gone in years. Mineral-associated organic matter is soil organic matter bound to mineral surfaces or locked in aggregates, crumbs of soil particles stuck together. That protects it from decomposers, and it can persist for centuries. Particulate organic matter, mostly little-decomposed plant remains, lasts only years to decades. Mineral influences dominate the carbon held deeper in soil, which helps explain why more carbon is stored at depth.

nature-eco-397.title: Mycorrhiza: the fungus-root partnership
nature-eco-397.text: Most tree species and many crops have fungal partners in their roots, but the cabbage family does not. Such a partnership is a mycorrhiza, a union of fungus and plant roots that benefits both. The fungus takes carbohydrates from the root. In return it supplies the plant with nitrogen, phosphorus and moisture. The fungus either sheathes the root, as in ectomycorrhizae, or enters root cells as branched structures called arbuscules, as in arbuscular mycorrhizae. Chemical signaling between plants through shared fungal networks remains a matter of conjecture.

nature-eco-395.title: Nitrification: turning ammonia into plant food
nature-eco-395.text: Ammonia gas is toxic to plants, so converting it matters. Nitrification is the step of the {{ref:nature-eco-176}} in which soil bacteria turn ammonium from decaying proteins into nitrates that plants can take up. Small groups of bacteria and archaea carry it out, using oxygen. It runs in two stages. Bacteria such as Nitrosomonas turn ammonia into nitrite, and others such as Nitrobacter turn nitrite into nitrate. Nitrosomonas is an autotrophic nitrifier: it makes its own carbohydrate without sunlight.

nature-eco-396.title: Denitrification: returning nitrogen to the air
nature-eco-396.text: In waterlogged soil, some bacteria breathe nitrate instead of oxygen. Denitrification covers the processes in oxygen-poor soil that turn nitrates and nitrites back into nitrogen gas or nitrous or nitric oxide, returning nitrogen to the air. It is done mainly by bacteria such as Pseudomonas and Paracoccus, which live without oxygen or can switch to doing so. Too much of it depletes soil nitrogen and fertility, and excess nitrogen fertilizer can cause it. It also has uses. Because it removes nitrate and reduces leaching to groundwater, it can treat sewage and high-nitrogen animal waste.

nature-eco-394.title: Nitrogen fixation: pulling plant food from the air
nature-eco-394.text: Lightning fixes between 5 and 10 billion kg of nitrogen a year, but bacteria called diazotrophs do most of the work. Nitrogen fixation is the conversion of nitrogen from the air into nitrogen compounds that living things can use. Plants cannot take up the nitrogen in air until it has been fixed. Some fixers live freely, such as Azotobacter and cyanobacteria. Others, the rhizobia, live in root nodules of legumes such as peas and beans. Nitrogen-fixing bacteria also play a decisive role in the early formation of soil.

reviews.ecosystem-structure-and-function: Every ecosystem runs on producers, which capture sunlight or chemical energy and build the biomass that all other organisms depend on. Only about ten percent of that energy passes from one trophic level to the next, which keeps food chains short and lets a few species, such as keystone predators and ecosystem engineers, reshape whole communities. Species share their habitats by occupying different niches, and their interactions run from competition and predation to mutualism. Underfoot, decomposers and soil organisms turn the dead back into the nutrients and organic matter that keep soil fertile, closing the loop that primary production began.
